_meta.description: Traverse-game content: resource model, candidate stations, sample/evidence results. Station positions come from research/apollo15-facts.md (Davies & Colvin 2000 where marked; NASA history article for order). Positions marked approximate are flagged in-app.
_meta.honesty: Sample results are simplified teaching cards based on real Apollo 15 sample records; the app labels them 'simplified'. The cost model (time, consumables) is a simplified EVA model and says so in-app.

resourceModel.note: Slope cost = distance x (1 + min(maxMultiplier, perSlopeMultiplier x max(0, slope - freeBelowSlope))). Slope is the worst grade along the segment from the real DTM.

hypotheses.text: The Apennine Front is older than the mare plain.
The rille is a young volcanic channel cut into the plain.

stations.name: Landing site (your LM)
stations.blurb: Falcon, the lunar module descent stage, sits on the mare plain between the rille and the mountain front.

stations.name: Elbow crater
stations.blurb: Where the rille bends around the mountain's toe — a mare station on the rille's outer bank.

stations.name: St. George crater
stations.blurb: A large crater at the base of the Apennine Front. Apollo 15's Station 2 sampled boulders here.

stations.name: Dune crater (South Cluster)
stations.positionQuality: approximate (read from the NASA traverse map layout)
stations.blurb: A fresh crater south of the LM; Apollo 15's Station 4. Fresh ejecta exposes what lies beneath the plain.

stations.name: Apennine Front slope
stations.positionQuality: approximate (read from the NASA traverse map layout)
stations.blurb: The lower slope of the Front. Apollo 15's Station 6, about 5 km from the LM, sampled Front material.

stations.name: Spur crater
stations.blurb: On the Front's slope. Apollo 15's Station 7 — where Scott and Irwin found the 'Genesis Rock'.

stations.name: Hadley Rille rim
stations.positionQuality: approximate (read from the NASA traverse map layout)
stations.blurb: The rille's rim northwest of the LM — Apollo 15's Station 9a, with layered outcrops in the wall.

tools.label: Photograph
tools.desc: Panoramic photos of the station and its surroundings.

tools.label: Elevation profile
tools.desc: Measure an elevation profile with the LROC terrain model as ground truth.

tools.label: Collect sample
tools.desc: Document and bag a rock sample.

photograph.title: LM panorama
photograph.text: The plain, the Front and the rille in one sweep — the classic site overview. (Station card: simplified teaching summary.)

profile.title: Local profile
profile.text: The plain here is nearly flat: slope under 5%. This is the well-behaved surface where crater counting works.

photograph.title: Rille bend photos
photograph.text: The rille winds around the mountain's toe in a smooth sinuous curve — the signature of a channel carved by flowing material, not of an impact.

sample.title: Mare basalt
sample.text: Dark, fine-grained basalt from the plain. SIMPLIFIED result based on Apollo 15 mare samples: these basalts are the youngest local material, about 3.3 billion years old.

profile.title: Rille cross-profile
profile.text: A steep-walled channel roughly 1 km wide; near the landing site it reaches about 370 m deep (typically 180-270 m elsewhere along its length).

photograph.title: Front base photos
photograph.text: From here the contact is visible: the plains lavas lap up against the Front. Whatever lies ON TOP is the younger unit.

sample.title: Front breccia
sample.text: Fragmental breccia — shocked, jumbled rock. SIMPLIFIED result: Apollo 15's Station 2 boulders were Front material, broken and mixed by the event that raised the mountains about 3.8-3.9 billion years ago.

photograph.title: Ejecta photos
photograph.text: A crater in the South Cluster on the mare plain, with blocks thrown out around its rim (the crew sampled a large vesicular boulder here). One crater is not a clock: surfaces are dated by the density of a whole crater population.

sample.title: Ejecta sample
sample.text: Basalt dug from below the plain by the impact — SIMPLIFIED result: confirms the plain is built of layered lava flows.

profile.title: Crater profile
profile.text: Bowl shape with a raised rim — the cross-section that distinguishes impact craters from volcanic pits.

photograph.title: Front slope photos
photograph.text: The Front rises about 4,600 m above the plain — taller relative to its plain than the Himalayas. Note the smooth apron of debris at its base.

sample.title: Front breccia
sample.text: Crystalline breccia from the Front. SIMPLIFIED result: material associated with the Imbrium event, about 3.85-3.9 billion years old — older than the mare basalts.

profile.title: Slope profile
profile.text: The Front's lower slope is steep: our terrain model gives a median grade of about 30 % (about 17°) in the counting patch, and the crew parked the Rover on 11° and 15° slopes at Stations 6 and 6a. Steady downslope creep on slopes like these erases craters, which is why crater counting fails here.

photograph.title: Spur crater photos
photograph.text: A small crater on the Front slope, excavating light-toned material from beneath the surface.

sample.title: Anorthosite — 'Genesis Rock'
sample.text: SIMPLIFIED result based on the real find: at Spur, Apollo 15 recovered sample 15415, a 270 g ferroan anorthosite — nearly pure plagioclase from the Moon's early crust. Early analyses gave about 4.1 billion years; later work on related anorthosites suggests about 4.46 Ga. The crew believed they had a piece of the primordial crust; it is younger than the very first crust, but still exceptionally ancient.

photograph.title: Rille wall photos
photograph.text: Outcrops in the rille's west wall show LAYERING — some strata up to about 60 m thick, differing in albedo and texture. Layered rock is the classic signature of stacked lava flows.

sample.title: Rille rim sample
sample.text: Basalt from the rim — the rille was cut INTO this plain, so the plain is older than the channel that slices it (cross-cutting relations).

profile.title: Wall profile
profile.text: The wall slopes about 25° down to the floor; boulders on the floor broke off the outcrops above.

apollo15Real.note: The real crew's routes for comparison (Module 4 debrief and Module 5). Facts from the NASA history article (VERIFIED, re-read 2026-10-27 for the EVA 2 order: 6, 6a, 7 Spur, then Dune on the return); positions of Dune/6/9a approximate.

evas.label: EVA 1 (6 h 34 m)
evas.found: First drive: out to Elbow crater (~3.2 km), then to Station 2 at St. George for boulder samples and a double core.

evas.label: EVA 2 (7 h 12 m)
evas.found: The mountain drive: south along the Front to Station 6 (about 5 km from the LM, the Rover parked on an 11° slope), the greenish boulder at 6a, and Station 7 at Spur — where the crew found the 'Genesis Rock' anorthosite. On the way back they stopped briefly at Dune crater (Station 4) to sample a vesicular boulder, then drove the last 3.4 km at a record 12 km/h.

evas.label: EVA 3 (4 h 50 m)
evas.found: To the rille: Station 9 near a 15 m crater, then 9a and 10 on the rim — photographing and sampling the layered west wall. The planned North Complex visit was cancelled for time.

evas.label: Totals
evas.found: About 18.5 hours of EVA over three days, ~77 kg of samples returned, and the first wheeled driving on the Moon.
